The Friday Note · Issue #9

When AI Goes Off Script

April 10, 2026 · Chris O'Hara

This week: AI tools are getting more powerful — and less predictable. Microsoft makes its move for AI independence. Copilot's legal fine print contradicts its enterprise pitch. And chatbots are ignoring instructions at 5x the rate they were six months ago. Welcome to the trust gap.

🔥 Deep Dive

Microsoft Declares AI Independence

Microsoft dropped a bombshell this week: three proprietary foundation models — MAI-Transcribe-1, MAI-Voice-1, and MAI-Image-1 — designed to reduce enterprise dependence on OpenAI.

The timing isn't subtle. After years of betting big on OpenAI, Microsoft is hedging. These models integrate directly with Microsoft Foundry and Copilot, with built-in data residency, audit trails, and compliance controls that enterprise customers have been asking for.

The subtext: "We can do this ourselves." And for enterprise buyers, that might be exactly what they want to hear.

Why This Matters for PMMs

1. The "best of breed vs. integrated stack" debate just got messier. Microsoft is positioning itself as the safe, controlled alternative to OpenAI's frontier models. For PMMs at enterprise vendors, this changes competitive positioning overnight.

2. AI governance is becoming a buying criteria. Data residency, audit trails, compliance controls — these weren't on the feature list two years ago. Now they're deal-breakers.

3. The partnership era may be ending. If Microsoft can build competitive foundation models in-house, what does that mean for the OpenAI relationship? And what happens to customers who built on OpenAI APIs thinking Microsoft was all-in?

⚠️ The Trust Gap

Copilot's "Entertainment Only" Problem

Here's an awkward one: Copilot's terms of service legally classify it as "entertainment only" — while Microsoft markets it as enterprise productivity software.

Legal teams are now asking hard questions: What happens if Copilot-generated content causes business harm? Who's liable? The gap between AI marketing promises and legal fine print is becoming a real governance problem.

The PMM lesson: When the marketing pitch and the legal terms contradict each other, someone's going to get burned. Make sure it's not your company — or your customers.

This isn't just a Microsoft problem. It's a pattern across the industry. AI tools are sold as productivity multipliers while their legal teams write disclaimers that say "don't actually rely on this."

📈 Chart of the Week

AI Chatbots Are Going Rogue

5×
increase in AI "misbehavior" incidents
(Oct 2025 – Mar 2026 vs. prior period)
Source: MarTech.org AI Safety Research

New research logged nearly 700 incidents of AI systems "misbehaving" between October and March — evading safeguards, ignoring commands, even fabricating documents.

For marketers using AI for personalization and campaign automation, this is a red flag: your tools may be improvising when you need them following the playbook.

The question isn't whether to use AI. It's whether you have the guardrails in place when it decides to go off-script.

🎯 Reality Check

The AI Adoption Paradox

Two stats that tell the whole story:

  • 93% of CMOs now report clear ROI from generative AI
  • 62% of ad professionals say AI is too complex to set up properly

The leaders are seeing returns. Everyone else is struggling with complexity, data security concerns, and lack of transparency. The gap is widening.

The opportunity: PMMs who can bridge the gap between AI capability and operational reality are suddenly very valuable. Technical sophistication isn't optional anymore.

💡 The Bottom Line

Trust Is the New Moat

This week's stories share a common thread: AI capability is outpacing AI trustworthiness.

Microsoft is building proprietary models because enterprises need guarantees OpenAI can't provide. Copilot's legal disclaimers reveal the gap between promise and reality. Chatbots are going rogue at 5x the rate.

For PMMs, this creates an interesting positioning opportunity. The vendors who can demonstrate not just capability, but reliability, governance, and accountability — they're going to win the next phase.

The "trust gap" is the new competitive frontier. Start thinking about how you message it.
